messages.subject: primate surveys and Distance software
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am interested in using Distance to analyze the data I
collected on a primate survey this summer.  I'm a first-time
user and have run across a variety of viewpoints about
eliminating duplicate sightings before entering the data
into Distance.  However, I have yet to talk to anyone who
has actually used the program.

Does Distance compensate for multiple sightings of the same
group (cluster) on different days?  In the "New Project set
up Wizard" if I don't use a multiplier and instead directly
insert the transect effort, does that affect the ability of
the program to compensate for repeat sightings of the same
group on different days?

I will gladly compile the responses I receive if others are
interested.

Thank you,
H Matthews
matth...@winthrop.edu

--

If you walk the same line twice, just enter effort as twice the line
length, and pool the sightings data from the 2 days.  Distance does not
assume independence between the separate days if you enter the data this

messages.subject: Evasive movement 2 - further adventures in distance sampling
messages.subject_clean: Evasive movement 2 - further adventures in distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
The following is an edited transcript consisting of an email about
approaches to dealing with evasive movement I sent to the list a few
weeks ago and the subsequent discussion which Len and I had by email
(I've pasted the emails in order) - hopefully by posting this other folk
who have encountered similar problems may be drawn into a fruitful
exploration of the topic and lead to some defendable solutions...

=20

=20

=20

Hi all,

=20

Our aerial survey data of seaducks show evidence of evasive movement in
response to the plane (and the surveyors describe this too). This is
combined with a limitation in the data collection, since the observers
cannot see the sea surface beneath the plane to a distance of 44m either
side. The data are collected as cluster sizes in 4 bands which get wider
with distance from the plane.

=20

The problem is that an unknown proportion of the birds underneath the
plane are moving away from the flight path into the visible area,
leaving an equally unknown proportion behind. In addition there appears
to be evasive movement in the visible area too, with band B being higher
than band A.

I've looked through the archives for ways to tackle this kind of
problem, and none of the entries quite seem to match this problem.

=20

So far my approach has been to reduce the observation distances and
cut-points by 44m prior to analysis and assume that detection at 44m is
1 (although this obviously ignores the higher peak in B). To account for
the rising numbers between A and B I have fitted a haz-rate function
which splits the difference. However, I am concerned that I am risking
over-estimation of D, since the plane may have effectively squeezed all
the birds present near the transect (but un-observable) into a smaller
(but observable) area (i.e. the strip beneath the plane is 'empty' and
the surveyed area next to the plane has elevated numbers).

=20

I have been trying to come up with solutions to this based on the area
surveyed etc but have no solid answers yet.

=20

One I idea I had was if I could manually add 44m to the estimate of ESW
and then re-calculate D - would this only be valid under the assumption
that all birds have moved out of the 'blind' strip? (if so then this may
be a moderately acceptable assumption to make). If this is ok then I am
not sure how to re-calculate the variance estimators...=20

=20

Any help gratefully received.

=20

Mark

------------------------

=20

Len:

Did you get any responses to your evasive movement question?

-----------------------------

=20

No help has been forthcoming on the evasive movement question, and I
have to run a bunch of analyses before the end of the week so I have
plumped for a fudge adjustment - assume all the birds (of this
particular species) move out from the blind strip into the first two
bands in response to the plane, thus biasing the density estimate high.
So I add the half(width) of the blind strip to the ESW (post estimation)
and then re-calculate the density based on this new ESW. As far as I
could make out the variance in ESW is not affected by this modification,
so the 95ci just need to be re-calc with the new values for C and D
(using the eqn in the book).=20

I predict you're now going to give me half a dozen reasons why this is
statistically bunk and I am going to have a nightmare rest of the week
trying to come up with something better ;-)

----------------------------

=20

Hi Mark,

Sorry, as you predicted I think your suggested approach won't work -
here's why. If all birds move out into the first two bands then the true
distribution of birds with respect to the trackline is no longer uniform
- density is higher in the first two bands than the outer two. Distance
will interpret the steeper drop-off in counts between the inner two
bands as the outer two bands as a steeper detection function, and will
therefore under-estimate p, and therefore overestimate D. So, you will
have a double-overestimate: once because of the extra birds in the first
two strips and second because of the under-estimated p. The first
overestimate you compensate for by widening the strip post-hoc, but the
second you do not account for.

One solution if you believe that g(x)=3D1 out to the boundary of the
second strip would be to treat the survey as a strip transect from right
under the plane out to the boundary of the second strip. This would
result in a negative bias if (i) not all birds flushed from under the
plane and/or (ii) g(x)<1 out to the second strip boundary. It would be
an overestimate if any birds fly from the second band to the third or
farther band in response to the plane. Having independent information
about bird movement in response to the plane would help address these
issues, as it would give you a model for the distribution of birds with
respect to the plane when the plane flew over. Any of that about?

- Len

=20

and then:

=20

I had a further think about the evasive movement question last night,
and the only thing I can think of if you're not willing to assume that
g(x)=3D1 at the 2nd bin endpoint is to try some simulations to look at =
the
potential biases.  The problem is that there are several biases and they
are pulling in different directions.  Best would be to get some info on
duck movement.  Might be worth posting a summary of what you did and
what we've discussed back to the list and see if anyone else gives any
further feedback. =20

Cheers,

=20

 - len

----------------------

=20

=20

=20

Hi len

=20

Further complications/issues have now surfaced! Last thing yesterday I
ran a larger analysis on a combined dataset stratifying by region. The
combined observations do not show the rising frequency I have seen up to
now with smaller datasets from other areas, and so the globally fitted
det-fn has a much better fit to the data...so am now left wondering
about the extent of the evasive movement which had appeared to be an
important issue.

=20

It is possible that the datasets I've been looking at up to now (and
which we've been discussing) are from areas with low densities and more
'flighty' (!) populations, or from periods when the birds are more
easily disturbed.

=20

However, given the reasonable likelihood of movement from under the
plane and my current inability (your simulation ideas notwithstanding)
to know how to allow for it, I will use the strip trans approach to spit
out the preliminary results I need.=20

=20

Cheers

m

------------------------

=20

=20

Here's how I see it:

=20

- if you can assume that all birds flush from under the plane into the
first two distance bands, and that g(x) at the end of the second
distance band is 1 then a strip transect analysis with strip width equal
to the distance to the end of the second distance band is appropriate -
if you can assume that all birds flush from under the plane, but don't
want to assume that g(x) is 1 at the end of the second distance band,
then you may consider a line transect analysis of the data, assuming
that the beginning of the first band is 0 distance.  You then
re-calculate density to account for the area under the plane - e.g., by
taking area surveyed as transect length * (ESW + distance to beginning
of band 1).  A problem with this, as I explained before is that you may
over- or under- estimate density of animals in the distance sampling
part due to the movement.  So, if g(x) at the end of the second bin is
close to 1, then the first option, above, is safer.

 - if you can assume no birds flush from under the plane, but that some
do move within distance bands, you can use the above analyses but
without adding in the surveyed area under the plane.

 - if some proportion of animals from under the plane move then it's
hard to know what is best!

=20

Does this clarify things?

=20

 - Len

=20

-------------------------------

=20

=20

So - does anyone have any further thoughts on this problem?

=20

--

messages.subject: Questions about year effects and dependent estimate
messages.subject_clean: Questions about year effects and dependent estimate
messages.body_plain:
Hello List,
I have run into a couple of snags in the analysis of the data for my=20
graduate project and was wondering if anyone might have some insights into=20
a couple of matters. Let me quickly bring you up to speed.  I am analyzing=20
data from 2 yrs of songbird point counts in p-j and sage from southern=20
CO.  My design consists of four treatment types:  treated pinyon,=20
untreated pinyon, treated sage, and untreated sage.  Within each treatment=20
type I have 3 sites (for a total of 12) and within each site I have 12 or=20
15 points depending on the size of the site.  Each point was visited 4=20
times during the month of June in both years (total of 8 visits).  In=20
addition I collected a number of covariates pertaining to weather and=20
habitat.  The objectives of my study are to identify the effects of the=20
treatment on various species=92 density and also to develop regression=20
models using the various habitat variables to explain density.  Hopefully=20
this background will prepare you for the laundry list of questions that=20
follows.

=20

The only way for me to construct meaningful habitat models for my various=20
species is to use densities generated at the point level.  Unfortunately=20
(or obviously), I do not have enough detections at a given point to=20
generate independent density estimates and thus must use h(0) from a=20
pooled detection function and the count at each point in order to estimate=20
density.  Some have suggested using a spatial variance/covariance term in=20
the actual habitat models.  I have also been pointed to the work from=20
Royle and the Advanced Distance Sampling book.  I am wondering on your=20
thoughts as to a workable solution to this problem.=20
In my analyses a number of the models selected as the top model have=20
covariates in them (generally only one, but with the 2 years combined I do=20
get a few more).  Bearing in mind my interest is in estimates at the point=20
level I am wondering if I need to be incorporating the parameter estimates=20
of the covariate terms in some way when I am taking h(0) from the=20
detection function.  It was suggested that I use the inverse of the CV=20
(which is presumably reflecting the influence of the covariate) as a way=20
of weighting my regressions in the habitat analysis to acknowledge the=20
uncertainty around the point estimates of h(0).=20
Finally, since I have 2 years of data I was hoping to look for a year=20
effect; however I am not certain of how to implement this analysis using=20
DISTANCE 4.1.  First, I am not sure whether year should be included as a=20
stratum, point, or observation level variable.  If it is an observation=20
level variable then I am assuming I will need to use a survey effort of 8=20
(and number my visits 1-8).  Entering it as a point level variable=20
maintains a survey effort of four and does not confuse the visits but I=20
believe may bias the results if it is not actually a point level=20
variable.  It has been suggested that I use year as my strata to examine=20
for effects.  If I do that I can no longer stratify by treatment (unless I=20
include treatment as a variable at either the point or observation level=20
and post-stratify or use as a covariate).  Thus in order to have both=20
treatment and year at the Region level it seems I would need to perform=20
separate analyses with no way of comparing whether stratifying by=20
treatment was more important than year or vice versa.=20
I=92m not sure if all of that will make sense right away, I seem to be=20
thinking and talking in circles with this stuff lately.  I appreciate any=20
help or suggestions you may be able to offer.

Thanks

Matt

=20

Matthew Williamson

Graduate Research Assistant

Department of Fishery and Wildlife Biology

Colorado State University, Fort Collins, CO 80523

Office: (970)491-5790

Cell:(970)412-0442

messages.body_plain:
Dear Mark et al.

Thanks, interesting.

I was struggeling with that very question myself since 2 years.

Unless the numbers moved by 44m can be corrected for by the 'true'
detectability (=lowering the moved numbers in the further out classes),
rather than moving them plain into the next distance bin, I would
suggest doing a simulation.

This simulation would involve a density run with uncorrected numbers,
with numbers moved by 44m, and with numbers moved by 44m but corrected
with an assumed/known detectability curve. So three runs in DISTANCE.

The truth between these three density estimates must then be somewhere
in between... Not sure how to assess that though. But at least on get's
the ranges and the effects of movement onto Densities that way.

Moving animals out by 44m might somewhat violate the g(0) assumption,
post-hoc ?

Any other ideas ?

Best regards to everybody

   F.

Falk Huettmann PhD, Assistant Professor
Biology and Wildlife Dept., Institute of Arctic Biology
University of Alaska Fairbanks AK 99775-7000 USA

messages.subject: Re: Questions about year effects and dependent estimate
messages.subject_clean: Questions about year effects and dependent estimate
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt, list,

Apologies for my posting of earlier today -- hit the wrong button and sent to
the list before I'd finished the message.  Here's a more complete version:

Here's my take on it; others may have different opinions.

Let's start by thinking about how you might go about answering your questions if
you were doing plot sampling -- ie were counting all birds within your points --
rather than distance sampling.  Then you have a standard nested experimental
design, with visits within years within points within sites within treatments.
Your first question was about a treatment effect.  To answer this you need to
decide what you're going to treat as a random effect and what you're treating
as a fixed effect.  Any basic stats book or course will deal with this.  For
example, if you're treating sites as random, you can then collapse all the
other stuff below that and your basic data are the density estimates per site;
you have a standard 2-way ANOVA-type setup with 4 treatments and 3 replicates
(sites) in each treatment.  To answer your habitat questions, you want density
by site (so pool everything below that), and then you'd do a regression-type
model with covariates for habitat and probably site and treatment.

Things get a bit more complex when we introduce distance sampling, becuase as
you rightly said, one usually doesn't have enough samples to estimate a
separate detection function by site (first question above) or plot (second
question above).  Instead, one usually uses the MCDS engine to fit covariates
to a global detection function, and then estimate detection function and
density by site (first question) or plot (second question) (for how to do this
in Distance, see Chapter 9 of the online manual, Estimating the detection
function at multiple levels).  One could also try things like a completely
stratified detection function stratified by treatment, with covariates for
habitat, etc within each treatment (if sample size is large enough for a
separate detection function in each treatment), and use AIC to tell whether
this is better than an analysis without the detection function strata.  In any
case, unless you estimate a separate detection function by site (first
question) or plot( second question) the estimates of h(0) for each site or plot
will not be independent of one another.  This means that simple regression
methods such as those outlined above are not strictly valid as they assume each
density estimate is independent.

There are several potential solutions to this problem:
(i) ignore it, on the basis that it won't have too bad an effect on inference.
If you ignore the problem, you will tend to select too complex a regression
model using AIC, as the analysis will think there are more independent data
points (densities) than there really are; you will also tend to get too narrow
a variance estimate for the same reason.
(ii) use a resampling approach to get at the difference between treatments --
this will get around the too narrow variance problem.  For example, define
delta12 as the mean difference in density between sites in treatment 1 and
treatment 2 from your data.  To get a resampling based confidence interval on
this difference, you resample the data (e.g., resample the plots with
replacement, or the sites, depending on what is the random effect) refit the
detection functions and calculate new density estimats and then calculate a new
delta12, repeat this process many times and this gives you a distribution of
delta12s which you can use to get confidence intervals.  This can easily be
generalized to getting paired differences between 4 treatments, etc.  I think
Robin Russell, who has posted to this list before, has been using this kind of
approach with similar data to yours so you can ask her for details  (search the
list archives for her contact info).  Since you're estimating a detection
function lots of times using the resampled data, you'll likely want to do this
outside of the Distance GUI, by calling the analysis engines directly -- I've
previously posted stuff on this, and there's now an appendix in the Distance 5
manual about how to do this.
(iii) potentially use the same kind of approach in the habitat regression
question.

The above (ii) and (iii) don't solve the non-independence related model
selection problem - I don't have any thoughts on how to address this, but I
think it's a minor issue.

You asked about inverse variance weighting the estimates of point density in the
regression modelling -- you could do this if you like (can get variance
estimates for density by point from Distance) -- should increase precision in
theory, but you still have the non-independence problem.  (I would use inverse
variance not inverse CV myself - not sure why 1/CV was suggested to you.)

You also asked about year effects.  Then you want an estimate of density by
point for each year, and you'd include year in your regression model.  If
bootstrapping by point, you want to make sure that if you select a point in
year 1 in a resample you also select the same point in year 2.  Perhaps you
meant including year as a covariate in the detection function, in which case it
doesn't matter what layer you include it in within Distance -- all covariates
apply to the observation relevant to them (i.e., detection function modelling
takes place at the level of the observation).

A minor last point: you referred to your data collection method as a "point
count", whenmost people who collect distance data from points call it "point
transects" or "variable circular plots".  Point count is the usual term for the
approach where you don't collect distances and end up with a relative index of
abundance.

Hope this makes sense -- typing in a bit of a rush.  Feel free to email back
with further questions (although I might be a bit slow in responding).

 - Len

messages.subject: Question on MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a probably stupid question regarding the estimate of the=20
detection function at multiple levels in MCDS engine.

I am analysing data of bird transect counts in Italy. My design consists=20
of 2 strata, which strongly differ regarding both birds density and=20
detectability, visited in two different seasons during one year. Among=20
the others, the objective of my study is to estimate bird population=20
size before and after the breeding season.
Given the current limit of Distance regarding nested design, I construct=20
a model using season as covariate and fitting separate detection=20
functions for each stratum.
My problem is that Distance estimates density at three different levels,=20
i.e. global, stratum and sample (transects), while I'm interested in=20
density estimates at season (covariate)  level. Probably I missed=20
something, but I read the on-line documentation (especially chapter 9 -=20
Estimating the detection function at multiple levels) and I could not=20
find any clue.
My question are:
1) Is this approach completely wrong? I.e., should I analyse the data=20
regarding the two strata separately, and then combine the estimates by=20
hand?
2) Is it possible to obtain stratum and global density estimates at=20
covariate levels using the above mentioned model?

I appreciate any suggestions.

Thanks,

Dimitri
